title: SpaceX launched Google AI chips to orbit with Planet Labs satellites
content:
Alphabet launched its homegrown AI chips into orbit on Thursday in a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, a step towards making data centers in space a reality.
The launch window opened at 11:15 am PT from Vandenberg Air Force Base in California's Santa Barbara County, with liftoff occurring without incident. SpaceX successfully deployed all payloads on board by 1 p.m. local time.
SpaceX has promoted supercomputers in space as the next frontier in artificial intelligence infrastructure, touting "infinite real estate" in orbit as a means of escaping the data center backlash on the ground. During the uncrewed Transporter-18 mission, SpaceX will carry Planet Labs satellites, including a solar-powered prototype equipped with Google's tensor processing units (TPUs).
The Thursday launch marks the first in-orbit test for Alphabet's Project Suncatcher, a "moonshot" initiative Google first revealed in November 2025. The company aims to develop reliable, solar-powered AI computing infrastructure that can operate continuously in space.
"Our team has confirmed contact with the satellite and it is operating as expected," Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher, wrote in a blog post following the launch. He called it the first step in a long-term research effort, "exploring whether space could one day host scalable machine learning infrastructure."
Alphabet is a significant investor in SpaceX, which went public in June in a record IPO, and the businesses are close partners even as their AI divisions compete with one another. Alphabet's stake in SpaceX is currently valued at over $82 billion.
In low Earth orbit, satellites can "access near-constant sunlight, generating up to eight times more solar power than on Earth," Alphabet said in the post. Eventually, they expect to be able to "link together multiple constellations of satellites, allowing them to manage larger AI workloads while in orbit."
The Google parent has already tested its TPUs running AI workloads in a facility at the University of California at Davis, but doesn't yet know how its chips will perform in the challenging conditions of low Earth orbit.
SpaceX, led by Elon Musk, has also announced that it plans to build and launch its own orbital data centers. They will be comprised of swarms of satellites the company develops in Redmond, Washington, equipped with graphics processing units and solar arrays it plans to produce with Tesla, Musk's automaker.
Earlier this year, Musk said data centers in space would be the cheapest way to train AI, "and that will be true within two years, maybe three at the latest." SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said at an event in September that the company will deploy "supercompute in space" in 2027.
Industry experts say space-based data centers represent a far-out mission, if they can even become feasible, in part because rocket launches remain capacity-constrained and expensive. Orbital data centers would also require cooling systems and chips that can withstand extreme temperatures, as well as protection from radiation. Clutter and orbital debris could also impede their viability.
The Transporter-18 flight was the second major launch in a single day for SpaceX, which also began transporting astronauts to the International Space Station from Florida's Space Coast for NASA with an earlier liftoff on Thursday, marking the start of a six-month mission in orbit.

report.summary: Google's TPU-powered prototype launched on a SpaceX rideshare with Planet Labs, beginning Project Suncatcher's first in-orbit test of space-based AI computing.
report.background: AI demand is straining terrestrial data centers, which face power, water, land and permitting constraints plus growing local backlash. Google unveiled Project Suncatcher in November 2025 as a moonshot to test solar-powered AI infrastructure in low Earth orbit, where satellites can access near-constant sunlight. The Transporter-18 rideshare gave Alphabet a low-cost first orbital experiment alongside Planet Labs satellites. SpaceX, meanwhile, has its own orbital data center ambitions and went public in June in a record IPO; Alphabet holds a SpaceX stake valued above $82 billion. The launch reflects converging trends: reusable rockets lowering access costs, TPU efficiency gains, and tech giants searching for new compute frontiers beyond Earth's grid.
key_points: A SpaceX Falcon 9 lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base on Thursday carrying Transporter-18 payloads, including a Planet Labs satellite with a solar-powered Google TPU prototype. SpaceX deployed all payloads by 1 p.m. local time, and Google's Project Suncatcher team confirmed contact with the satellite and said it was operating as expected.

The mission is the first in-orbit test for Project Suncatcher, Google's long-term research effort to see whether space can host scalable machine-learning infrastructure. Google has tested TPUs running AI workloads at UC Davis, but it does not yet know how the chips will perform under low Earth orbit's radiation, thermal cycling and vacuum conditions.

Google argues orbital compute could tap near-constant sunlight, generating up to eight times more solar power than on Earth, and eventually link multiple satellite constellations to handle larger AI workloads. That vision depends on solving power, cooling, radiation tolerance and inter-satellite networking at scale.

SpaceX is pursuing its own orbital data centers: GPU-equipped satellite swarms developed in Redmond, Washington, with solar arrays planned with Tesla. COO Gwynne Shotwell said SpaceX will deploy supercompute in space in 2027, while Elon Musk has claimed space-based AI training could become cheapest within two to three years.

Industry experts remain skeptical. Rocket launches are capacity-constrained and expensive, and orbital data centers would need specialized cooling, radiation shielding and debris protection. The test is a technical milestone, not proof that space-based AI infrastructure is commercially viable.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the launch shifts the infrastructure debate from land and power contracts to orbital engineering, giving Google and SpaceX early experimental data on radiation-tolerant accelerators, solar power and thermal management. Developers may eventually get new compute options, but near-term work will focus on constrained, remote and fault-tolerant AI rather than routine training. Regular users are unlikely to see orbital AI services soon; the more immediate effect is continued investment in terrestrial efficiency and energy sourcing. The test also raises policy questions around orbital debris, spectrum, launch capacity and who governs data centers in space.
report.tools: Follow Google's Project Suncatcher blog and Cloud TPU documentation for official updates; Planet Labs mission pages and open satellite imagery for payload context; SpaceX Transporter mission pages for launch data. For independent modeling, open-source Skyfield or Orekit can simulate orbits, while NASA and ESA radiation-test resources inform chip hardening. No open-source orbital TPU stack exists yet, so treat vendor claims cautiously.
